{{short description|American topologist and mathematician (1908–1967)}}
{{redirects here|William Claytor|the Department of Defense official and president of Amtrak|W. Graham Claytor Jr.}}
'''William Schieffelin Claytor''' (January 4, 1908 – July 14, 1967) was an American mathematician specializing in [[topology]].  He was born in [[Norfolk, Virginia]], where his father was a dentist.  He was the third [[African-American]] to receive a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]]. in mathematics, and published two papers in the [[Annals of Mathematics]].<ref name=tutor/>

==Education==
Claytor attended public schools in [[Washington, DC]] and also the [[Hampton Institute|Hampton Agricultural and Industrial School]] in Virginia. In 1928 he received his BA from [[Howard University]], where he had been taught by [[Elbert Cox]], the first African-American to get a Ph.D. in mathematics.  [[Dudley Woodard]], the second African-American to get a PhD in mathematics, was just setting up the graduate program in math at Howard, and Claytor earned his MA there in 1929, with a thesis supervised by Woodard.<ref name=MAA>[https://www.maa.org/programs-and-communities/outreach-initiatives/summa/summa-archival-record/william-claytor William W. Schieffelin Claytor] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191215192911/https://www.maa.org/programs-and-communities/outreach-initiatives/summa/summa-archival-record/william-claytor |date=2019-12-15 }} at the [[Mathematical Association of America]] (MAA)</ref>

Claytor obtained his Ph.D. from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1933 with the dissertation ''Topological Immersion of Peanian Continua in a Spherical Surface'', directed by [[John R. Kline]],<ref name=pioneer/> who had also supervised Woodard's thesis and was himself a student of [[R. L. Moore]] (of the [[Moore method]]).<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=359}}</ref>  Kline wrote to Moore saying: "Claytor wrote a very fine thesis. In many ways I think that it is perhaps the best that I have ever had done under my direction."<ref name=tutor>[http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Claytor.html William Waldron Schieffelin Claytor] at the [[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Parshall, Karen Hunger|author-link=Karen Parshall|title=Mathematics and the politics of race: The case of William Claytor (Ph. D., University of Pennsylvania, 1933)|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=123|issue=3|year=2016|pages=214–240|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.4169/amer.math.monthly.123.3.214|doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.123.3.214|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
 
In 1934, a paper based on Claytor's thesis appeared in [[Annals of Mathematics]], credited to Schieffelin Claytor.  In 1937, also in the Annals, he published the paper "Peanian Continua not Imbeddable in a Spherical Surface", also credited to Schieffelin Claytor.

==Academic career==
Claytor had taught at [[HBCU]] [[West Virginia State College]] for three years following his [[doctorate]], not being able to secure a job at a majority institution due to the prevalent racism of the era.<ref name=race>''[https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.4169/amer.math.monthly.123.3.214?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents Mathematics and the Politics of Race: The Case of William Claytor]'' by Karen Hunger Parshall, The [[American Mathematical Monthly]], Vol. 123, No. 3 (March 2016), pp 214-240</ref> At West Virginia his students included [[Katherine Johnson]] who later worked on the space program for [[NASA]].<ref name=tutor/>

Claytor applied for a National Research Council Fellowship to work at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (IAS), which at the time was housed in [[Princeton University]], but was rejected on racial grounds.<ref name=race/>  In 1937 he received a [[Rosenwald Fellowship]] at the [[University of Michigan]];<ref name=diaspora>[http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/claytor_wschieffelin.html Mathematicians of the African Diaspora] at the State University of New York at Buffalo</ref> he stayed there for several years, but was not allowed to attend research seminars.<ref name=pioneer>[https://www.archives.upenn.edu/histy/features/aframer/math.html Pioneer African American Mathematicians] at the University of Pennsylvania Archives and Records Center</ref> [[Oswald Veblen]] had finally been able to offer him a position at the IAS in 1939, independently of Princeton University, but Claytor turned it down.<ref name=tutor/>

During the years 1941–1945, Claytor served in the US Army, teaching in the Anti-Aircraft Artillery Schools in Virginia and Georgia.<ref name=MAA/>  In 1947 he joined the faculty at Howard, where [[David Blackwell]] was then chair of the department of mathematics.<ref name="NYT-Grime-2007-07-17">{{cite news | last = Grime | first = David | date = July 17, 2007 | title = David Blackwell, Scholar of Probability, Dies at 91 | work = New York Times | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/17/education/17blackwell.html | accessdate = August 22, 2010}}</ref> Claytor taught at Howard until his retirement in 1965, serving as chair himself along the way.<ref name=diaspora/>

On August 5, 1947,  Claytor married the psychologist Mae Belle Pullins, who also shared his love of mathematics. They had one daughter.  He spent the rest of his career at Howard, and despite making many well-received presentations at AMS conferences, he continued to suffer from racial discrimination and was not even allowed to stay in the hotels where the meetings were held.<ref name=unsung>[https://undark.org/article/unsung-william-waldron-schieffelin-claytor/ Unsung: William Claytor] by Sabrina Nichelle Collins, Nov 2, 2016</ref>

==Awards==
The [[National Association of Mathematicians]] (NAM) has a lecture series named after Claytor and Woodard.<ref>[https://www.nam-math.org/claytor-woodard-lecture.html Claytor-Woodard Lecture] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180301104116/https://www.nam-math.org/claytor-woodard-lecture.html |date=2018-03-01 }} at the National Association of Mathematicians</ref>

The [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS) has a mid-career research fellowship, the Claytor-Gilmer Fellowship, named after Claytor and [[Gloria Ford Gilmer]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=The AMS Claytor-Gilmer Fellowship|url=https://www.ams.org/programs/ams-fellowships/claytor-gilmer|access-date=2021-05-24|website=American Mathematical Society|language=en}}</ref>
